blocks.title: Central question
paragraphs: How does an applied force become a measurable voltage and then a live LabVIEW reading?

You are building a local IoT measurement node that can detect applied force. Before this measurement can be logged or sent to the cloud, the system must safely excite a load cell, amplify its very small voltage output, read the amplified voltage with Arduino, and display a trustworthy live value in LabVIEW.
This lab focuses on the local sensing and signal-conditioning layer. It does not yet upload force data to the cloud.

steps.label: Amplifiers
steps.detail: V2 and then V3 increase the signal.

paragraphs: LabVIEW does not directly measure force. It reads amplified voltage. Calibration is required to display force units.

blocks.failureMessage: Not yet. Trace the path from applied force to LabVIEW voltage.

fields.label: Why might the raw voltage across SIG+ and SIG- be too small to read accurately with Arduino?

paragraphs: Arduino's analog input has limited resolution. Amplifying a tiny sensor voltage allows more of the input range to be used, improving useful measurement sensitivity.

fields.label: AV1 = R3 / R1 (given R3 = 1 MΩ, R1 = 10 kΩ)

expected.message: Check the ratio: AV1 = R3 / R1 = 1 MΩ / 10 kΩ. Convert both resistors to the same unit first.

fields.label: AV2 = 1 + R6 / R5 (given R6 = 100 kΩ, R5 = 10 kΩ)

expected.message: Remember the extra 1 in the non-inverting gain: AV2 = 1 + R6 / R5 = 1 + 100 kΩ / 10 kΩ.
Cascaded stages multiply: AVtotal = AV1 × AV2 = 100 × 11.

checkpoints.title: Build the raw load-cell sensing circuit
intro: Use Arduino 5 V and GND, connect the load cell through screw terminals, and construct the initial circuit at the far end of the breadboard because later amplifier stages will be added.

blocks.title: Think it through
items: Which wires supply the load cell?

checkpoints.title: Measure the tiny differential output
intro: Put the load cell at the edge of the table, pin one end carefully, and apply force gently to the other end in the indicated direction. Record a range rather than trusting one reading.

blocks.title: Think it through
items: Is the raw signal single-ended or differential?
Is the no-load output exactly zero? Why or why not?
What might cause the reading to drift?
Why might hand-applied force produce inconsistent readings?
Why is this raw signal not yet ideal for direct IoT measurement?

checkpoints.title: Amplify the load-cell signal with the first op-amp stage
intro: Add the first-stage amplifier using the LMC6484. Use pin 2 for SIG-, pin 3 for SIG+, and pin 1 for output V2. Use R3 = R4 = 1 MΩ and R1 = R2 = 10 kΩ. The ideal gain is AV = R3 / R1 = 100.

blocks.alt: First LMC6484 amplifier stage for the load-cell signal.
blocks.caption: In the first-stage amplifier, R3/R1 sets the ideal gain of 100 for the V2 output.

paragraphs: Before connecting V2 to Arduino A0, verify that V2 remains within the Arduino analog input range.

blocks.title: Safe recovery sequence
paragraphs: Disconnect power before changing the circuit. Confirm the LMC6484 orientation and pin numbers, common ground, feedback path, and 10 kΩ/100 kΩ/1 MΩ resistor identities. Measure the output before reconnecting A0, and change one suspected fault at a time.

blocks.title: Think it through
items: Why do we amplify the load-cell signal?

checkpoints.title: Add a non-inverting second-stage amplifier
intro: Add the second-stage amplifier using op-amp number three on the LMC6484 chip, pins 8, 9, and 10. Use R5 = 10 kΩ and R6 = 100 kΩ. The additional ideal gain is AV = 1 + R6 / R5 = 11.

blocks.alt: Complete two-stage LMC6484 amplifier circuit connected to Arduino analog input.
blocks.caption: The non-inverting second stage increases V2 to V3 before Arduino A0 reads it.

paragraphs: V3 should be about 11 times greater than V2, subject to supply and saturation limits. Verify V3 is safe before connecting it to Arduino A0.

fields.label: Does your measured V3/V2 ratio support the expected gain of 11? Explain using your data.

blocks.title: Think it through
items: Why add a second stage instead of changing the first stage?
What does non-inverting mean?
Why is the gain 1 + R6/R5 rather than R6/R5?
What is the ideal total gain of the two stages?
What is op-amp saturation?
How could excessive gain make the measurement worse?

checkpoints.title: Display amplified voltage in LabVIEW
intro: Create a LabVIEW VI that reads the amplified signal on Arduino A0 and displays it with a numeric indicator named `Voltage Reading`.

blocks.alt: LabVIEW block diagram showing LINX Open, Analog Read channel 0, timing, stop control, and voltage reading indicator.
blocks.caption: Read Arduino analog channel 0 and display the amplified voltage.

paragraphs: Add a numeric indicator named `Voltage Reading`.
Use LINX Open, LINX Analog Read, While Loop, Wait Until Next ms Multiple, Stop button, and LINX Close.
Set Wait Until Next ms Multiple to numeric constant `100`.
Use Stop for normal shutdown and keep LINX Close after the loop.
Repeat force application and compare LabVIEW displayed range with voltmeter V3 range.

checkpoints.title: Redesign the circuit to halve total amplification
intro: The original ideal gains are AV1 = 100, AV2 = 11, and AVtotal = 1100. The halved ideal total gain is 550. Do not change the circuit while powered. Confirm modified resistor values and expected output range before reconnecting Arduino A0.
